title: A report on the state of the music market – 2007

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A revolution is happening in the way consumers obtain and pay for music, and the music business is transforming itself for the new environment. Like many revolutions, this is a continuous process and there are many divergent views within the industry on where it will end. The industry has always been known for being innovative and today its chief characteristic continues to be experimentation. Music is pioneering the advance of the creative industries into the digital world. The task of creating commercial value from online content or through mobile phones confronts a range of industries, from newspaper publishing to television and film. However, music’s market share is higher than in any other entertainment sector except games.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Record labels are proactively reinventing themselves, moving away from a record-based model, and diversifying their sources of revenue across a much broader range of products. Digital is no longer a separate component in the operation of a record company – it is wholly incorporated into all the products being offered and planned. A release from an artist today may appear in dozens, sometimes hundreds, of different digital products. Technology has enabled these changes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The consumer is king in the digital world, and entertainment spend is shared competitively among a wide range of products and services. Consumers’ time is also a valuable asset and industries are competing for their attention. Consumers have more choice than ever as to how they want to connect to and experience the music from their favourite artist – they can buy a download, a CD, wallpaper for their mobile phone, a mastertone, an e-ticket, a music video, become their friend on a social network or sign up to a subscription service. In many cases consumers will choose various products, and acquire these on many different platforms. Growing use of broadband mobile phones and portable devices has helped the launch of hundreds of digital music services. These have enabled consumers to refer to vast music catalogues that are far more extensive than the ones produced by traditional retail stores. The development of very small digital players with their enormous storage capacity has given music lovers instant access to their entire collection of songs wherever they go.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In addition to these benefits, the advances of technology have brought huge challenges. For one thing, ease of access to music has damaged consumers’ perception of its financial value. There have also been significant brakes on the digital music sector: the lack of interoperability between services and devices due to different providers’ security systems; proprietary software tied to particular brands of hardware, regardless of security systems; the lack of investment in marketing to promote new music services; and piracy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Widespread copyright theft continues to be the most significant barrier to the development of a legitimate digital music business. The mass availability of unauthorised, unpaid-for music has caused major damage to CD sales as well. Digital piracy is also developing into more varied forms, requiring more sophisticated anti-piracy enforcement strategies, and highlighting the critical need for increased cooperation from the internet’s gatekeepers, the Internet Service Providers (ISPs). 2007 has seen significant progress on both fronts. The Japanese recording industry has become the first to tackle public attitudes to mobile music piracy, launching a new, artist-led campaign for mobile phone users with the three biggest mobile carriers, called ‘Please protect mobile music’.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The digital music market in 2007 reflects both the progress of the industry and the very significant challenges that remain in creating a commercially successful digital music business. Record companies’ digital sales continue to grow strongly, but have not yet made up for the sharp decline in CD sales, resulting in a worldwide overall market decline in 2007. There are exceptions in some countries where digital sales have compensated for the decline of physical music products, led by Japan, the world’s second largest music market, and including markets such as India, China, Indonesia and South Korea.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: A fascinating example to the rest of the world is the case of Japan. It is the first market where full-track mobile downloads, as opposed to single ringtones, are the leading digital format, accounting for over 40 per cent of sales value. The mobile phone is the leading channel for entertainment and music there. Young people use their mobiles for multiple purposes, allowing on-the-go access any time and anywhere. Mobile phones penetration is widespread, with over 100 million mobile subscribers and 70 million users of 3rd Generation (3G) equipment. One key reason for the country’s digital market success has been the formation of a single mobile music retail service, jointly owned by record companies. This was established in 2001, and is today the leading provider of content to mobile operators. Local repertoire is strong: the big sellers in 2007 include GReeeeN, Utada Hikaru and RSP.
